An interesting Italian Violin by Luigi Speranza, Naivasho, Kenya 1944, labelled Speranza Luigi fecit Naivasha Kenia Anno 1944, the entire violin meticulously constructed from matchsticks, those of the back and ribs arranged in a herring-bone pattern, the back with diamond-shaped hardwood plaque inlaid P.O.W. 55213, length of back 14 1/16in. (357mm.)  This violin was made by an Italian prisoner-of-war held in British Camp 352 in East Africa. The instrument is sold with a letter from the Commandant of the camp, Lt.-Col. Murdock (?), dated 27th May, 1944, addressed to the Red Cross Shop in Nairobi. The letter states that the violin was made from 13,760 matches and took approximately three months to construct (See Illustration)

(358mm.), circa 1790, in case  James Sandy (b. 1766, d. 1819) lived his entire life in Alyth, Scotland, indeed he was a cripple and bedridden from the age of 12. Despite this handicap he achieved some considerable recognition, not primarily as a violin maker but as a practical mechanic and in particular the inventor of the hinge usually seen on the Laurencekirk type of snuff boxes. For an Article on his life and work entitled 'The Alyth Mechanist', see The Scots Magazine, July 1975 (See Illustration) (2)

A German Violin, labelled Antonius Stradivarius Cremona faciebat Anno 1723, the two-piece back of faint medium curl ascending from the joint, the ribs and the head plain, the table of broad grain, the varnish of an orange colour, length of back 14 1/8in. (358mm.) (2)
